name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,372

clue.text: Legendary bowler gets duck

blocks.note: first meaning: Sir Francis, said to have finished his game of bowls before facing the Armada

explanation.surface: A famous cricket bowler is dismissed without scoring.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of nothing, so the surface reads as a bowler out for zero; but the bowler plays bowls on Plymouth Hoe and the duck is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Francis Drake is the legend of the bowls green, and the male of the duck species shares the same word.

clue.text: Tired chap works for peanuts

indicators.note: to work something is to shape or knead it, so the letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: An exhausted man labours for a pittance.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting something for peanuts is an idiom for paying almost nothing, which is what dirt cheap describes.

clue.text: You'll find 12 in this, ultimately detailed?

definitions.text: You'll find 12 in this, ultimately detailed?

blocks.note: surface reading: the answer to 12 across is located inside this thing
setter's reading: a book that sets out every country in fine detail, the last word in reference for places

explanation.walkthrough: 12 across is a South American country, and the book where you look up any country is the one named after the Titan who held up the heavens.
explanation.definitionFit: An atlas is a bound collection of detailed maps, so every country, Paraguay included, can be found in one.

clue.text: Key Stage One accommodates new class

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room to a guest, so one piece holds another inside it

blocks.note: a stage of a journey or race is a leg
an ace is a one on dice or cards
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A first-year school group takes in a fresh form of pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: Key Stage One is the English school term for ages five to seven, so the surface is about schooling; here it splits into three separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Class in the sense of style or refined distinction is a synonym of elegance.

clue.text: Lively movement in Spooner's beer glass

indicators.note: Rev. Spooner was famed for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the two words trade their starts

blocks.note: bitter is a British beer and a jug is a glass vessel; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: Something lively stirs inside the Reverend Spooner's pint glass.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is an English pale ale.
explanation.definitionFit: The jitterbug is an energetic swing dance of the 1940s, so a lively piece of movement.

clue.text: Show surprise when Judd Trump misses middle pocket

indicators.note: a pocket of letters from the centre is missed out, leaving just the front and back

blocks.note: the snooker player's name taken as written

explanation.surface: A snooker champion is startled when his shot fails to drop into the centre pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: Judd Trump is a world snooker champion, and snooker tables have middle pockets, which makes the surface convincing; the pocket is just the central five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To start or flinch in surprise is to jump, as when someone jumps at a sudden noise.

clue.text: Recording includes Daniel Craig's first steps

indicators.note: something that includes another thing holds it inside
the first of Craig's letters only is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: A filmed record captures the actor Daniel Craig's first attempts at something.
explanation.walkthrough: Daniel Craig, the James Bond actor, is split into a short form of his first name and his surname's initial.
explanation.definitionFit: Tap dancing is a style of dance made of rhythmic footwork, so a set of steps.

clue.text: Tail deteriorate after losing wicket and appeal

indicators.note: losing something means it drops out of the word

blocks.note: to wear is to deteriorate with use
W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wicket

explanation.surface: A cricket side's lower-order batsmen crumble after a wicket falls to an appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail in cricket is the weak lower batting order, and an appeal is the fielders' shout for a wicket; both are misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: To endear is to win affection, much as something that appeals to you attracts and charms you.

clue.text: Type of seat found in bar perhaps, and in Paris, on reflection - without question

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the other pieces sit around it

blocks.note: to bar is to ban, one possible sense
QU is an abbreviation for question
et is French for and, followed by its mirror image

explanation.surface: A kind of seat is spotted in a pub, and in a Parisian café too, without any doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: On reflection works like a mirror placed after the French word, so it is followed by its own reversed image. The bar is the verb, to forbid, not the pub counter.
explanation.definitionFit: A banquette is an upholstered bench seat, often built along a wall in restaurants and bars.

clue.text: Good morning - I say, how's your bad leg?

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
my is an exclamation of surprise, like I say

explanation.surface: A cheery greeting from someone enquiring after a friend's injured leg.
explanation.walkthrough: Gammy is British informal for lame or injured, used almost only of a leg, which is why the clue ends on one.
explanation.definitionFit: A gammy leg is a lame or injured one, so in this informal usage the word means bad or crippled.

clue.text: It charts the highs and lows of English film drama - gather round

definitions.text: It charts the highs and lows

indicators.note: a drama is a staged commotion, a sign the letters are thrown into disorder
to go round something is to enclose it

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
to reap is to gather a harvest

explanation.surface: Something tracks the ups and downs of British cinema drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The highs and lows sound like the fortunes of the film industry, but they are hills and valleys.
explanation.definitionFit: A relief map shows terrain elevation with shading or raised contours, charting mountains and valleys.

clue.text: Material that's hard to see in space? On the contrary

indicators.note: the contrary of A in B is B in A, so the outer and inner parts swap roles

blocks.note: dim light makes things hard to see
an en is a printer's space

explanation.surface: A fabric that is difficult to make out in outer space, or the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, dim goes in en; on the contrary flips it, so en goes inside dim.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is a sturdy cotton twill fabric used for jeans, so it is a material.

clue.text: Money's short, unable to be spent frequently - that's careless

indicators.note: something short is missing its end

blocks.note: U/S, unserviceable, is military shorthand for unusable

explanation.surface: Cash is running low and can't be used often, which is sloppy budgeting.
explanation.walkthrough: CAS is cash cut short; USUAL loses US, the unserviceable label, leaving UAL. The parse is loose: nothing in the clue signals that second removal.
explanation.definitionFit: Casual can mean offhand or lacking due care, a close synonym of careless.

clue.text: Country park mostly indistinct, having no boundaries - area unknown

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
without its boundaries a word loses its first and last letters

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for area
in algebra x, y and z are unknowns

explanation.surface: A national park is hazy and unfenced, its extent uncharted.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraguay is a landlocked nation in South America, bordering Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia.

clue.text: Appearing at last, chicken tikka's pink when cooked - call for a bit of service?

indicators.note: only what appears at the very end of each word is kept
cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are mixed into a new form

blocks.note: to ring is to call on the phone

explanation.surface: A curry arrives undercooked, so a diner calls a waiter over.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of tikka's means is: the last letters come from chicken and tikka. A service here is a set of tableware, not waiting staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A napkin ring holds a rolled table napkin and belongs to a dinner service, one small item of table setting.

clue.text: Looking ahead, Essex Police cut administration, continually being decentralised

indicators.note: with the centre removed from each word, only the outside letters are left

explanation.surface: A county police force, planning for the future, keeps trimming its central bureaucracy.
explanation.walkthrough: Essex is a county east of London. Decentralised sounds like a policy of devolving power, but it strips the middle from five words.
explanation.definitionFit: Expectancy is a state of anticipation, the attitude of someone looking ahead to what will come.

clue.text: With vigour, I consumed Argentine food

indicators.note: what is consumed is swallowed, so it ends up inside the other pieces

explanation.surface: Someone eagerly devoured a meal from Argentina.
explanation.walkthrough: PEP with I is the container; Perón, Argentina's mid-century leader, goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepperoni is a spicy cured sausage, eaten on pizzas, and so an item of food.

clue.text: Character not the first to get urge

indicators.note: leaving out the first means the opening letter is lost

blocks.note: a witch is a stock character of fairy tale and pantomime

explanation.surface: A personality, though not the leading one, develops a yearning.
explanation.walkthrough: Several characters will lose a letter to leave this answer (Witch, Mitch, Titch); the deletion matters, not which one.
explanation.definitionFit: An itch is a restless desire or craving, as in an itch to travel, so it is an urge.

clue.text: Extremes of Australian bush unfortunately not the best for dairy farming

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters
an unfortunate outcome is things going wrong, so these letters are muddled
the best is A1, and not having it means those characters leave the word

explanation.surface: The edges of the Australian outback are poor country for raising dairy cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means first-rate, and in crosswords it is written AI, so removing it from dairy leaves DRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Husbandry is the care and breeding of crops and livestock, an old word for agriculture.

clue.text: Where you'll get seconds - doughnuts one 21 picked up

indicators.note: in a down entry, picking something up lifts it so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: 21 down is a journalist, and an editor, ED, is one

explanation.surface: A bakery offers second helpings: doughnuts and more.
explanation.walkthrough: Seconds are a boxer's helpers in the corner, not second helpings of doughnuts.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer's seconds attend from the corner just outside the ropes, which is the ringside position.

clue.text: Leaving jacket, nipped out for a smoke?

indicators.note: a jacket is an outer covering, and leaving it off removes the outside letters
out here means out of place, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Someone took off their coat and slipped outside for a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipe is a smoking device, and to have a pipe is to have a smoke of tobacco.

clue.text: They may come across a school where truants hide in the back of cupboard

definitions.text: They may come across a school

indicators.note: whoever hides something keeps it inside them
the back of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: a skiver is British slang for someone dodging work or school

explanation.surface: A teacher may stumble on a school's absentees hiding at the back of a cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: The school is a shoal of fish, not a place of truancy.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin-divers swim underwater without a diving suit and may well swim past a school of fish.

clue.text: Girl taking pot with old hack

blocks.note: an urn is a pot or vase
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A young woman smokes cannabis with a veteran writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Pot sounds like the drug; it is a vessel. Taking simply places it after Jo.
explanation.definitionFit: Hack is slang for a run-of-the-mill reporter, and journo is the informal word for a journalist.

clue.text: Sort of material found in corset - needing to be used regularly, having put on weight

indicators.note: using every other letter at a regular interval picks out alternate characters
putting on weight means the weight goes into the middle

blocks.note: the odd letters, taken until the run is complete
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A fabric for underwear must be worn regularly by someone gaining weight.
explanation.walkthrough: The alternate run through corset and needing yields C, R, E, N, E and then stops; TON goes in after the third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cretonne is a heavy printed cotton fabric used for upholstery and curtains, so a sort of material.

clue.text: Piece of meat that's medium on the inside - one needs to chew hard

indicators.note: something on the inside is placed within the other piece

blocks.note: a chop is a cut of meat
M is the abbreviation for medium

explanation.surface: A steak cooked medium inside is tough, so a diner must work their jaw.
explanation.walkthrough: Medium sounds like how the meat is cooked; it is the clothing-size abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To chomp is to munch noisily and vigorously, chewing hard on food.

clue.text: Creature's droppings mostly deposited in middle of aviary

indicators.note: mostly means all but the end, so the final letter goes
what is deposited in something is set inside it
only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: guano is bird or bat droppings
the central pair of six letters

explanation.surface: An animal's excrement lies in the centre of a birdhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's means has, linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An iguana is a large tropical lizard, so it is a creature.

clue.text: Looking for a publication on climbing

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing goes upward, so the word reads bottom to top

blocks.note: the FT is the Financial Times newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone wants a magazine about mountaineering.
explanation.definitionFit: To be after something is an idiom for seeking or pursuing it, as in the police are after him.

clue.text: Prejudice shown when in support of substantial cut

indicators.note: in a down entry a supporting piece sits underneath the other
a cut word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Favouritism appears when backing big reductions in spending.
explanation.definitionFit: Bias and prejudice both mean an unfair leaning toward or against someone.

clue.text: Being old and moody, one might hit you in the nose

definitions.text: one might hit you in the nose

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A grumpy elderly person might punch you on the nose.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads like a punch from a grumpy pensioner, but a smell hits you in the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong smell is said to hit you, and the nose is where it lands, so an odour fits.

clue.text: Current delay is over - without it having started

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the delay goes around it
turned over, the word is flipped to read backwards

blocks.note: I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: The current hold-up has ended, though nothing has yet begun.
explanation.walkthrough: I is the physics symbol for electric current. The delay holds the next word inside it before the whole thing is turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: Initiated means begun or set in motion, so a thing that is initiated has started.

clue.text: Soaps go in for dramatising unseen killer

indicators.note: dramatising reworks material into a new shape for the stage

explanation.surface: TV soap operas love staging a mystery murderer nobody sees coming.
explanation.definitionFit: Poison gas is often colourless and invisible, so it kills without being seen.

clue.text: First? Almost not the first

indicators.note: without its first, the word loses its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they came first and is told they very nearly did, but not quite.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a looser definition: the first to arrive is early.
explanation.definitionFit: Early can describe what comes first in time or order, like the early chapters.
